:::{#thm-gram-invertible}
#### $\tp{\mX}\mX$ is invertible when $\mX$ has full column rank

If $\mX$ is an $n \times p$ matrix with $\operatorname{rank}(\mX) = p$ (@def-rank),
then the $p \times p$ matrix $\tp{\mX}\mX$ is invertible.

:::

::: proof
Let $\vecf{c}$ be a vector of length $p$ with $\tp{\mX}\mX\vecf{c} = \vzero$.
Then

$$
\ba
0
&= \tp{\vecf{c}}\,\tp{\mX}\mX\vecf{c}
&& \text{(multiply } \tp{\mX}\mX\vecf{c} = \vzero \text{ on the left by } \tp{\vecf{c}} \text{)}
\\
&= \tp{\paren{\mX\vecf{c}}}\paren{\mX\vecf{c}}
&& \text{(transpose of a product)}
\\
&= \norm{\mX\vecf{c}}^2
&& \text{(definition of the Euclidean norm)}
\ea
$$

so $\mX\vecf{c} = \vzero$.
Because $\mX\vecf{c} = c_1 (\text{column } 1) + \cdots + c_p (\text{column } p)$
and the columns of $\mX$ are linearly independent,
$\vecf{c} = \vzero$.
So the only solution of $\tp{\mX}\mX\vecf{c} = \vzero$ is $\vecf{c} = \vzero$,
which says that the columns of the square matrix $\tp{\mX}\mX$ are linearly independent,
and a square matrix with linearly independent columns is invertible
[@banerjee2014linear, Corollary 5.7, p. 143].
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-gram-invertible}
#### Inverting $\tp{\mX}\mX$

For the rank-$2$ matrix
$\mX = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$
from @exm-rank:

$$
\tp{\mX}\mX = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ 6 & 14 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\inv{\tp{\mX}\mX} = \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix} 14 & -6 \\ -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix},
$$

and multiplying the two out gives $\matr{I}_2$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-hat-matrix}
#### Hat matrix

For an $n \times p$ design matrix $\mX$ (@def-design-matrix)
with $\operatorname{rank}(\mX) = p$,
the **hat matrix** is the $n \times n$ matrix

$$
\underbrace{\matr{H}}_{n \times n}
\eqdef
\underbrace{\mX}_{n \times p}
\underbrace{(\tp{\mX}\mX)^{-1}}_{p \times p}
\underbrace{\tp{\mX}}_{p \times n}
$$

The inverse exists by @thm-gram-invertible.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-hat-matrix}
#### The hat matrix of an intercept-only model

With $n = 2$ observations and only an intercept,
$\mX = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ ($2 \times 1$, rank $1$),
so $\tp{\mX}\mX = 2$ and

$$
\matr{H}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \cd \frac{1}{2} \cd \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then $\matr{H}\vy = (\bar{y}, \bar{y})$, where $\bar{y} = (y_1 + y_2)/2$:
the fitted values of an intercept-only model are the sample mean.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-hat-matrix}
#### Hat matrix is a projection matrix

If $\mX$ is an $n \times p$ design matrix with $\operatorname{rank}(\mX) = p$,
then the hat matrix $\matr{H}$ (@def-hat-matrix)
is an orthogonal projection matrix (@def-projection-matrix).

:::
